headline: Rebuild What People Hate but Can't Quit Paying For
lede: Greg Isenberg, CEO of Late Checkout and former advisor to Reddit and TikTok, published a detailed six-step playbook in January 2026 for building a $10 million app portfolio in a year by rebuilding existing mobile apps with AI. The argument is not about invention but renovation: find software users tolerate despite loathing it, strip out the friction, and pocket the delta. The post reached one million views, suggesting it hit a nerve among a generation of builders newly equipped with AI coding tools.
body:
The core thesis rests on a counterintuitive signal: apps with sub-4-star ratings and strong retention. Most product thinking chases love; Isenberg chases **grudging dependency**. A user who pays $15 a month for a clunky utility they curse at every morning is, in his framing, a better commercial signal than a delighted user of something free. He recommends filtering Sensor Tower — a mobile analytics platform used by app marketers and investors — for apps earning $50,000 to $200,000 in *monthly recurring revenue* (MRR, the annualized subscription income from active subscribers) with stagnant interfaces and minimal update histories. The metric he prizes above all is revenue per download, which strips out vanity downloads and reveals whether users stay and pay.

The alarm clock example is real. The image attached to the post shows a Sensor Tower entry for *Alarmy*, made by Delight Room Co., Ltd., a South Korean developer, recording 500,000 worldwide downloads and $500,000 in revenue in a single month. Alarmy succeeds not by invention but by solving one problem more aggressively than the default: it forces users to complete physical tasks — scanning a barcode, solving a math problem — before the alarm stops. Isenberg's point is that this kind of absurdly narrow improvement, executed by a small team, now generates eight-figure annual revenue.

The AI layer is not about building new AI products; it is about collapsing manual steps inside workflows that already charge for time savings. He lists the telltale targets: apps where the core experience is 'upload and wait,' dashboards that show data but make users decide what it means, and services that advertise 'analysis' but rely on humans behind the scenes. **AI fits best when it collapses steps, not when it replaces judgment entirely** — a useful heuristic that keeps the thesis grounded. Turning a raw input into a clear recommendation, or flagging what matters rather than showing everything, is the kind of upgrade he targets.

Distribution is treated with equal seriousness. Isenberg recommends finding niche creators — photographers, designers, writers — who use a tool daily but have never made a video about it, then paying roughly $5 per thousand views (*CPM*, cost per mille, the standard ad-pricing unit) to seed *UGC*, or user-generated content: authentic-looking short videos made by real users rather than a brand. TikTok Shop, he notes, has made this loop commercially efficient for consumer apps.

The endgame is a **holdco**, or holding company — a portfolio of small apps sharing infrastructure, cashflow, and distribution muscle rather than a single product bet. Each acquisition funds the next. The model is less Silicon Valley venture swing than private-equity roll-up applied to the App Store's long tail, a structural shift enabled by AI development tools dropping MVP costs from hundreds of thousands of dollars to, in his rhetorical shorthand, almost nothing.

concepts.definition: A metric that divides total app revenue by total downloads over the same period. Unlike raw download counts, it reveals whether users stay long enough to generate subscription income — a signal of genuine stickiness rather than viral curiosity.

The predictable, subscription-based income a software product earns each month. Investors and founders use it to assess business health because, unlike one-time sales, it compounds: a stable MRR base grows without constant re-acquisition spend.

A marketing strategy that pays ordinary users — not professional advertisers — to create short, authentic-seeming videos about a product. On platforms like TikTok, UGC often outperforms polished ads because it fits the native format. Brands typically pay creators per thousand views (CPM) rather than a flat fee.

A holding company that owns and operates a portfolio of small software applications rather than building a single large product. Cashflow from early apps funds later acquisitions; shared code, infrastructure, and distribution create compounding advantages across the portfolio.

Isenberg's term for the pattern of an app with poor user ratings but high retention and consistent revenue — indicating users need the tool badly enough to keep paying despite a poor experience. He treats this as a renovation opportunity rather than a reason to avoid the market.

fact_check: Isenberg writes: 'Wealthfront is the Robinhood of Canada. Does ~$200M in revenue with $50B under management.' This is almost certainly a confusion of names. **Wealthfront** is a US-based robo-advisor, majority-owned by UBS since 2022, and is not Canadian. The company he likely means is **Wealthsimple**, a Toronto-based fintech that has frequently been described as Canada's answer to Robinhood and Betterment and that manages tens of billions for Canadian retail investors. The revenue and AUM figures cannot be verified from the provided sources, but the company name appears to be an error.
